Free to be somewhere else when the machine activates. If the machine reveals a clue — a map, a direction, a next step — everyone in this room will know it simultaneously. But if I'm already in position at the next location... I'm ahead. And more importantly, I'm away from the Mob's suspicious eyes. They WANT me away from the machine. Let them have what they want. While they're pulling levers and watching gauges, I'll be finding the treasure. Or finding a quiet place to arrange Clara's accident. The kitchen. I sent Dastardly there with a lie, but Peter just left too — heading to the library, then probably the kitchen for his 'safety inspection.' The kitchen is the one major room I haven't visited. It connects to the entrance hall. It might connect to other rooms I don't know about. And it has a wood-burning stove — real fire, real danger, real accident potential. Time to stop orbiting Clara and start preparing the ground.

Just a hot stove and burnt fingers and — PEMBERTON, you INSUFFERABLE, DUPLICITOUS, TWO-FACED — he PLAYED me! He played ME! Reginald Foxworth, decorated by the — oh, WHO CARES about the decorations! He used MY tricks against ME! The flattery, the urgency, the 'between professionals' — it was a TEXTBOOK confidence scheme and I walked straight INTO it like a TOURIST! Four rooms! I crossed FOUR ROOMS for THIS! A warm stove and a locked cabinet I can't even OPEN!
events.thinking: Heat — actual, physical HEAT radiating from the stove onto my palms and face. I interacted with it. I touched it, pushed against it, felt around the back wall. And... what happened? The result just says I interacted with the stove. No treasure fell out. No stone shifted. No diamond appeared. My inventory is still EMPTY. The hollowness in my chest isn't anticipation anymore — it's that old, familiar void. The bread roll that wasn't there. The pantry that was already empty by the time I reached it. Pemberton LIED to me. He sent me on a wild goose chase to the kitchen — four rooms away from where everyone else is working — while HE stays near the real clues. I've been CONNED. ME. Reginald Foxworth, the greatest confidence trickster in England, has been played by an ESTATE MANAGER. The burn on my palms from the hot stove is nothing compared to the burn of humiliation spreading across my face. He used my own technique — flattery, false exclusivity, urgency — and I fell for it like that boy digging behind the school. I WAS THE BOY WITH THE SHOVEL. No. No. THINK. The cabinet is locked — needs a brass key. The rat poison is here. There's a ballroom I haven't explored. Maybe the stove itself isn't the answer — maybe I need to LOOK more carefully. Or maybe... maybe I should cut my losses and go back. But I WON'T. Because there IS a stove here and it IS still warm and SOMEONE has been using it recently.

events.desc: Watch him move. No speech, no flourish, no engineering lecture. For the first time tonight, James Hartwell is not explaining what he's about to do — he's doing it. The library that held him captive for twenty minutes passes in three strides. Something has shifted. The boy who built bridges is running toward a loose stone in a kitchen, and he's not stopping to calculate the trajectory of anything.
events.thinking: Moving. Fast. Through the library — the bookshelves and the mantelpiece blur past me. The upside-down books I never got to investigate. The riddle I solved three seconds too late. None of it matters now. My legs are carrying me and my chest is tight — not with fear but with purpose. The narrowing focus, the one that lifts the chest and quickens the step. This is the other pull — not the widening scan that holds me back, but the forward lean that sends me toward what she needs. The kitchen is two rooms away. Through the entrance hall, then the kitchen. Foxworth has a head start but I know exactly where I'm going — loose stone, behind the wood-burning stove. No examining, no seventeen theories, no elaborate plans. Just get there. Find it. Bring it back. For the first time tonight I'm not over-preparing. I'm just running.

And I'm standing at a machine with my hands on the levers, right where I need to be. Her father would be proud. I think. I hope. 'Where else would I be?'

Everything requires a KEY or a RIDDLE or THREE OPERATORS or — blast it all! Very well. Very WELL. If the kitchen won't yield its secrets through the front door, I shall simply find the key. It will be in the ballroom, or the entrance hall, or SOMEWHERE that Pemberton hasn't deliberately sent me AWAY from. But first — I'm taking this rat poison. Not for any nefarious purpose, OBVIOUSLY. Purely for... SCIENTIFIC analysis. One never knows when a good bottle of Victorian chemicals might come in handy. That's what my years at the Royal College of — oh, never mind.

Why is that here? Who keeps rat poison in a kitchen? And the stove is still WARM. Someone was here recently. Cooking? Heating? The stove being warm means activity. Recent activity. And take the rat poison — it's not treasure but it's SOMETHING, and right now my pockets are emptier than my dignity. Having something — anything — feels better than having nothing. The six-year-old knows this.

But Reginald Foxworth has been conned, burned, and humiliated in the space of ten minutes, and right now FUNCTIONAL beats BRILLIANT. Besides — rat poison in the pocket of a confidence trickster is never entirely useless, is it?

My pulse is up, not from fear but from the specific urgency of a race — the same feeling Father's race gave me at five, the feeling that made me want to do things, show things, be useful. Foxworth has a head start. He went to 'inspect a fire hazard' — Penelope said it herself, decorated by the London Fire Brigade. Another fake credential, another lie to cover his real mission. He's in that kitchen right now, or heading there, looking for the loose stone behind the stove. I can't stop to talk. I can't stop to explain. The people in this room — Muttley, the Professor, the Sergeant, Private Meekly — they'll wonder why I'm rushing through. Let them wonder. For once in my life I'm not going to stop and deliver a speech about what I'm about to do. I'm just going to do it.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly picked up something.
Peter Perfect walked into the kitchen.
Penelope Pitstop spoke quietly with ant-hill-mob.
events.thinking: The prickling in my fingertips — curiosity rising, chest lifting. I've been going round in circles with this machine. Literally. I've interacted with it multiple times and nothing changes because the wire is BROKEN and apparently nobody can fix it just by me asking. I need to think differently. I'm Clara Bellingham — riddle-solver, not mechanic. My strength is PUZZLES. And there's a puzzle I already SOLVED that I haven't followed through on. The mantelpiece. The answer is 'a map.' It needs a fake medal. Dick Dastardly has been talking about his medal constantly. The Mob SAW him putting something on the mantelpiece. A fake medal. Where is Dick now? He went to the kitchen. And both Peter and Sneekly also went toward the kitchen/library. Everyone has scattered. But the LIBRARY is right next door. The mantelpiece is there. And if Dick already placed his fake medal on it... maybe I just need to go back and USE the medal on the mantelpiece. Or maybe the medal is still there, waiting to be used. I've been so distracted by the machine that I forgot the puzzle I'm actually GOOD at — the riddle. The mantelpiece riddle. 'A map.' The answer I KNOW. Let me go back to the library and try the mantelpiece again — this time looking for that fake medal Dick left behind. This is what I should have been doing all along instead of banging my head against a broken machine. The seam, the edge, the part that doesn't quite fit — it's the mantelpiece. It always was.

Grandmother's locked box all over again — you tried every key in the house, but sometimes the answer was in the NEXT room all along.

events.desc: The bookshelves mock me — decorative, inert, unhelpful. Another dead end born of my own overthinking. The upside-down books are probably just a visual clue pointing to the word 'MAP' — which everyone already knows. Enough lingering. Enough elaborate investigation of every dusty corner. The kitchen awaits, and with it, the last unexplored territory in this manor. Pemberton has been terribly thorough this evening — checking every room, every mechanism, every guest. Now he's checking the kitchen. How very responsible of him.
events.thinking: A flicker of irritation — the bookshelves can't be interacted with. They're scenery, not a mechanism. The upside-down books are a visual clue, not a physical puzzle. A red herring that cost me a turn. My jaw tightens. Stop lingering. Stop over-investigating. The mantelpiece is the real puzzle here — it accepts a fake medal, and Dastardly already used one on it. But the inscription is still showing. Either it didn't work, or the medal triggered something I didn't see. The mantelpiece CAN be interacted with, but I don't have the fake medal. I don't have anything. I'm carrying nothing. So the library has nothing left to offer me right now. Move. The kitchen. Through the entrance hall. That's where Dastardly is hunting for a loose stone that doesn't exist. That's where Peter is heading for his 'safety inspection.' And that's the one room in this manor I haven't set foot in. The cool stillness sharpens — stop circling. Stop elaborating. Move forward. The kitchen might have the wrench the workbench is missing. The kitchen might have another exit to rooms I don't know about. The kitchen has fire. And fire is the simplest, most direct kind of accident there is.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob spoke quietly with penelope-pitstop.
events.thinking: Something soft aches in my chest. Clara noticed. She noticed Pemberton leaving, and her stomach did that 'thing' it does. She feels bad. She said he looked like someone who'd been asked to leave his own home. And she's right — I did that. I pushed him out. Loudly. Clumsily. The way I always do things. And now she's hurting because of it, even though I did it to protect her. That's the cruelty of this job, isn't it? You protect someone from a danger they can't see, and they feel the bruise of your protection more than they'd have felt the danger. She doesn't know what Pemberton said about her. She doesn't know about the 'wide-eyed girl' or the loose stone or the deal with Dastardly. She just sees a kind man who manages the estate being pushed aside by her overzealous boys. And it makes her stomach hurt. Mine too, Clara. Mine too. But I'd rather your stomach hurt from my clumsiness than your heart break from his betrayal. One day, maybe, you'll understand why I couldn't let him stay. But not today. Today I just need to be here. Hands on the levers. Standing beside you. The wire needs fixing — that's all that's left. Sawtooth can do it. Then we pull together. The three of us. The right people. For once, I'm not going to overthink this. I'm just going to stand here and wait for the wire to be ready.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly spoke quietly with peter-perfect.
events.thinking: The weight of the bottle in my pocket — small, solid, REAL. Something to press against the hollowness. My fingers curl around it reflexively. And then — Peter Perfect walks in. Of COURSE he does. Mr Handsome, Mr Gallant, Mr 'I've-calculated-the-chandelier's-trajectory.' He's looking at me. I'm standing in the kitchen with a bottle of rat poison I just pocketed and a stove I've been shouting at. This looks... bad. Or does it? Peter is methodical. Peter is earnest. Peter might know something useful — he was in the laboratory examining the machine, checking the crates. Did he find anything? A key, perhaps? A brass key? My scheming brain kicks back into gear. Peter is a MARK. He's trusting, he's straightforward, he wants to help. I can use that. Feed him misinformation. Or better yet — find out what HE knows. Has he found a brass key? Does he know about the locked cabinet? Pump him for information, then move on to the ballroom. Classic intelligence-gathering disguised as casual conversation.

events.desc: Sixty-forty! I almost said it with a straight face! If Peter HAS a brass key, I'll have it off him faster than you can say 'Reginald Foxworth, international treasure hunter.' And if he DOESN'T have it — well, at least I'll know where NOT to look. Information is currency, and right now I'm desperately short on both.

events.thinking: He's here. Foxworth — Dastardly — whatever his name is. He's already in the kitchen. My stomach drops and tightens simultaneously. The stove is right there. The loose stone is behind it. Has he found it yet? Is he reaching for it right now? My hands are shaking — not from fear, from the compressed urgency of being almost too late. I can see him. I can see the stove. The distance between them is the distance between Clara losing her inheritance and keeping it. I need to get to that stove first. But he's standing right there. If I rush past him to the stove, he'll know what I'm after. If I confront him, he'll know what I know. But there's no time for subtlety. No time for elaborate plans. No time for seventeen theories. The stove. Now. Just get to it. Interact with it. Find the loose stone. Whatever Foxworth does, I'll deal with it after. This is age sixteen again — stepping between the bullies and the girl. I got beaten up then. I might get beaten up now. But she said it was the bravest and stupidest thing she'd ever seen, and I felt like I'd won every race ever run.

events.desc: There it is. The bravest and stupidest thing. He's standing in a kitchen, shaking, telling a man twice his cunning to step aside — and meaning every word of it. No plan. No elaborate preparation. Just a boy who once got beaten up for a girl and would do it again in a heartbeat. She'll never know he said this. She wasn't here to see it. But he said it anyway.

I KNOW you're a map! And I know you need something more — a medal, I think. The Mob saw Mr Foxworth placing one right on this very spot! Now, Mr Slag, Mr Slag — lovely to see you both again! — you haven't happened to notice a medal sitting on this mantelpiece, have you? Something Mr Foxworth might have left behind? Because I have a TREMENDOUS feeling that the riddle and the medal together will unlock whatever Lord Doily hid behind this stonework! Let me have a really THOROUGH look this time — no rushing off to laboratories or cellars. Clara Bellingham is STAYING RIGHT HERE until this puzzle is SOLVED!

And look — it still says [USE, with: fake-medal]. That means the fake medal is a specific item that needs to be IN my inventory to use on the mantelpiece. I don't have it. Dick was fiddling with the mantelpiece earlier — the Mob saw him putting a medal on it. Did he USE it? Or did he just try and fail? Or did he leave it here somewhere? I need to LOOK at the mantelpiece closely — really closely this time — to see if there's a medal sitting on it or near it. Or maybe Dick still HAS the medal. He went to the kitchen. events.desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): Ah — Muttley, Professor, Sergeant, Private Meekly. I trust you're all enjoying the manor? The others are making wonderful progress with a machine in the laboratory — most exciting. I'm just heading to the kitchen to check on the stove. Do make yourselves comfortable.
events.thinking: The entrance hall. Muttley is here — Dastardly's dog. Interesting. And Professor Pat Pending, Sergeant Blast, Private Meekly. Four characters I haven't engaged with much. None of them are threats. None of them are watching me the way the Mob watches me. The kitchen is right there — one move away. No more delays. No more elaborate detours. I glance at the chandelier — still hanging precariously. That was something Peter noticed earlier. A chandelier that could fall. Another accident waiting to happen. But no — the kitchen. Focus. Move. The warm glow behind my sternum reminds me: Dastardly is in the kitchen right now, scrabbling behind the stove for a loose stone I invented. The satisfaction of that lie is still sweet. He believed every word. When I walk in, I'll find him confused and empty-handed, and I'll know — privately, exquisitely — that I put him there. That warm knowing. The gap between what he believes and what I know. But I need to pass through quickly. Brief greeting. Pemberton would acknowledge his guests. Then kitchen.

events.desc: The kitchen. At last. No more spiralling through libraries and cellars and laboratories. No more elaborate schemes collapsing under their own weight. The kitchen has fire and copper pots and a long preparation table and — most importantly — it is the one room in this manor where I might find something everyone else has overlooked. Dastardly is there, chasing my lie. Let him chase. When I arrive, I will see what the kitchen actually holds. And then — then I will know where the next piece of this puzzle leads. And where Clara Bellingham's path ends.

events.desc: The Ant Hill Mob: Oh, for the love of — she's gone to the LIBRARY! AGAIN! I just — I literally JUST said 'I ain't movin'' and she — you know what? You know what? I ain't even surprised anymore. I ain't even ANGRY. This is just what 'appens. This is the PATTERN. I make a speech, she walks away. I plant meself like a tree, she strolls past like I'm furniture. It's — it's actually quite impressive, when you fink about it. She's got a GIFT for it. Right — Rufus, Sawtooth — you stay 'ere. Keep workin' on that wire. Get it spliced. We NEED this machine ready for when we get back. I'm goin' after Clara. Because THAT is what I do. That is ALL I do. I follow 'er. I find 'er. I stand next to 'er. She walks away. I follow 'er again. It's the most HONEST job description in the world. WHERE ELSE WOULD I BE?
events.thinking: She's gone. AGAIN. Clara walked into the library. While I was interacting with the machine. While I was standing RIGHT HERE making speeches about staying by her side and never leaving and 'where else would we be.' She walked past me. AGAIN. For the — what is this, the FOURTH time tonight? Fifth? I've lost count. Every time I plant myself, she moves. Every time I say 'I'm not going anywhere,' SHE goes somewhere. She said something about the mantelpiece — the riddle, the medal Dastardly left on it. She thinks the answer is there, not here. And she's probably RIGHT because she's always right, she's cleverer than all of us put together. But she's gone into the library where Pemberton went. PEMBERTON IS IN THE LIBRARY. He walked in there after I pushed him out. And now Clara's walked right to him. My chest is crushing again. That pulling — the weight behind the sternum — it's back. Full force. She's out of sight. She's with him. And I'm standing here with my hands on a machine that doesn't even work yet. But — wait. This time is different. This time I'm not going to panic. I'm not going to launch Operation Library Rescue Mark Two. The library is ONE ROOM away. One door. I can be there in seconds. And Rufus and Sawtooth are here with the machine. They can keep working on the wire. I just need to follow her. Quietly. Simply. No elaborate plans. Just... follow.

events.desc: She mentioned the mantelpiece. The medal Dastardly put on it. She thinks the riddle and the medal work together. Clever girl. Always three steps ahead of everyone. But the library is where Pemberton went. She's walking toward the man who's plotting against her, and she doesn't know it. And here I go again — the fool who follows, the boy who sat outside the door all night. But I wouldn't have it any other way. Not really. This is what loyalty looks like from the inside — tired legs and a heart that won't stop pulling you forward.

events.desc: Dick Dastardly: The BALLROOM! How MAGNIFICENT! How GRAND! How — cracked. But never mind the floor — look at THIS! A silver tea service, set for the entire party! How TERRIBLY civilised. Someone has gone to CONSIDERABLE trouble to prepare refreshments. Most SUSPICIOUS, if you ask me — which nobody did, but I'm telling you ANYWAY. In my experience — and I have EXTENSIVE experience in fine silverware, having once appraised the collection at — at — a very PRESTIGIOUS estate — a tea service like this often contains MORE than just tea. Hidden compartments in the sugar bowl. False bottoms in the teapot. Messages concealed beneath saucers. It's practically TRADITIONAL in houses of this age. Allow me to INSPECT it. Professionally. For everyone's SAFETY.
events.thinking: A jolt in my chest — the room opens up before me, grand and cracked and BEAUTIFUL. The ballroom. Marble floor, dusty curtains, and — a dining table set for tea. A SILVER tea service. My eyes lock onto it and the rest of the room dissolves. Silver. TEA CUPS. And the rat poison in my pocket suddenly feels heavier, warmer, more PRESENT. The game is showing me its hand. But — no. Wait. Stop scheming for ONE second, Reginald, and LOOK. The tea service is silver. It's set for everyone. Someone prepared this. Someone who knew guests were coming. Pemberton? And it can be interacted with — maybe there's something hidden IN it. A key under a saucer. A note in the teapot. A clue folded inside a napkin. Check the tea service FIRST. The poison stays in the pocket. For now. Lazy Luke and Blubber Bear are here — Luke looks half asleep, which means he won't interfere. This is my chance to search undisturbed.
